\subsection{The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses}
\seclabel{revival-meet}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{more-specific-rule}; \secref{overloading-static-params};
\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}; and, in a draft build, the proposed
features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] Where the Meet Rule for functions, or for functional methods,
asks for a declaration on the intersection of two parameter types, declarations
whose parameter types are each a subtype of both and together cover the
intersection also satisfy it, every pair of those declarations satisfying the
rules in turn; the case does not apply to the condition on the types from which
the two parameter types define coercions.
A box at the rule answers the draft note that asks what the intersection of two
declarations is; the Meet Rule of \secref{overloading-static-params} gains the
same case, with a box.
The Meet Rule's example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and that $f(V)$
is applicable to and more specific for any call at run time to which $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$ are applicable.
\secref{principles-overloading} says that a static call whose argument's static
type stands between a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types
may have several declarations applicable to it that no other applicable
declaration is more specific than, and is not a static error.
The second of the two facts of \secref{overloading-coercion-resolution} keeps a
single most specific declaration for the dynamic call and, but for such a call,
for the static call; the declaration that the dynamic call runs is the same as
or more specific than every declaration applicable to the static call, its
return type a subtype of theirs; the type of a static call whose most specific
declarations, and every declaration more specific than them that the call may
run, have no static parameters is the intersection of their return types; and a sentence gives the scope of the proof.
In the internal document, the proposed feature on the intersection of two types
with \KWD{comprises} clauses is marked done.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the Meet Rule gains the case of declarations that
together cover the intersection, and that a call whose argument's static type
stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses is typed by the
intersection of its candidates' return types, with the proof of
\appref{overloaded-functional} revised to the uniqueness of the most specific
declaration at run time (\secref{revival-proof}).
The team's list of proposed features records the same plan for the example:
``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check''.
Under the reading of \secref{trait-decls}, the intersection of two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses is not in general equal to a named type, and without the
case the Meet Rule would refuse the example given to illustrate it.
The case is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011,
which asks for a declaration on the meet, as the type group's calculus
Welterweight Fortress does (\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-meetrule.tick},
in the revival's repository).
The typing of such a call follows from the Return Type Rule: the declaration
that runs is below every most specific declaration of the static call, and its
return type below each of theirs.
For a declaration with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
one of those return types at once, which the proof does not show, so the typing
is stated for declarations without static parameters only.
The covering is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
subtype of another.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md} in
the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The Meet Rule's example is valid; both implementations refused it
before this change (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).
A static call whose argument's static type stands between two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses, as an instantiation of a trait with static parameters
that extends both unlisted does, is not a static error: it runs the declaration
that covers its value, and, where those declarations and every declaration more
specific than them that the call may run have no static parameters, its type is
the intersection of the return types of its most specific declarations.
The compiled type checker departs from this in four ways: it types such a call
by the intersection only in a family none of whose declarations has static
parameters, and otherwise by one of its most specific declarations (row~543 of
the revival's gap ledger); its code generator stops at a method call on a value
of such a type (row~540); it refuses the case for declarations with static
parameters (row~546); and its verdict on a trait between the two that provides
both declarations of a functional method can depend on the components it
compiled before (row~547).
The Meet Rule for dotted methods keeps its form, asking for a declaration on the
intersection (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft's rules are unchanged, the cases being
added after them.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines 303--307,
the example's conclusion:
\begin{quote}
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$ ``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more specific for any call to which both

The intersection of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any subtype of every type $T \in S$ and of the intersection of every
subset of $S$ is a subtype of $U$.
Similarly, the union of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any supertype of every type $T \in S$ and of the union of every
subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.

A type $U$ \emph{covers} a type $T$ when every value of $T$ is a value of $U$.
A type covers each of its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause
is covered by the union of the types listed in the clause
(\secref{trait-decls}).
Covering is a relation between the values of types and not the subtype
relation: a type may cover another type that is not its subtype.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not define
covering.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) names covering beside
subtyping and exclusion as a relation between types, and says that an
instantiation of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union of
the listed types.}
For example:
%trait S comprises {U,V} end
%trait T comprises {V,W} end
%trait U extends S excludes W end
%trait V extends {S,T} end
%trait W extends T end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any value of both $S$ and $T$ is a value of
$V$.  Thus, $V$ covers $S \inter T$.
A trait may stand between $S$ or $T$ and their listed types
(\secref{trait-decls}), so $S \inter T$ is not in general equal to a named
type.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 concluded that
any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$, so that
$V = S \inter T$.

%trait V extends {S,T} end
%trait W extends T end
%
%f(s:S) = 1
%f(t:T) = 1
%f(v:V) = 1
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(s\COLONOP{}S) = 1\)\\
\(f(t\COLONOP{}T) = 1\)\\
\(f(v\COLONOP{}V) = 1\)
\end{Fortress}
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any value of both $S$ and $T$ is a value of
$V$.  Thus, $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$
``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and $f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more
specific for any call at run time to which both $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are
applicable.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 concluded that any
subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$, so that $V = S \inter T$.
That holds of types only while no type stands between $S$ or $T$ and their
listed types; a trait with static parameters may (\secref{trait-decls}), and a
static call whose argument has such a type has $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ applicable and
$f(V)$ not.
It runs $f(V)$, and its type is given in
\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}.}

The Meet Rule shall not be difficult to obey, especially because
the compiler can give useful feedback.  For example:

of them.
Where the declarations applicable to a static call that no other applicable
declaration is more specific than, and every declaration more specific than them
that the call may run, have no static parameters, the type of the static call is
the intersection of their return types; where there is one such declaration,
that is its return type.

\appref{overloaded-functional} formally proves that
the rules discussed in the previous sections guarantee the static resolution of
coercion (described in \secref{resolving-coercion}) is well defined
for functions (the case for methods is analogous).  Also in
\appref{overloaded-functional} is a proof that
the overloading rules for
 function declarations are sufficient to guarantee no
undefined nor ambiguous calls at run time (again,
the case for methods is analogous).
That proof covers declarations without static parameters and calls to which
declarations are applicable without coercion, and it rests on every value of a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause being a value of one of its listed types
(\secref{trait-decls}); the appendix states its scope.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that a single
most specific declaration is applicable to every static call to which any is
applicable, and that the one the dynamic call runs is more specific than it.
With the closed-trait case of the Meet Rule, a static call whose argument's
static type stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses and their
listed types may have several; the declaration that runs is below every one of
them, and the call's type is the intersection of their return types, which the
Return Type Rule makes sound for declarations without static parameters.
For declarations with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
one of those return types at once, and the type of such a call is not yet
given.
The compiled type checker does not yet enforce across components that every

\section{Proof of Overloading Resolution for Functions}
\seclabel{proof-overloading-resolution}

This section proves that the overloading rules for
function declarations are sufficient to guarantee no undefined nor
ambiguous call at run time (the case for methods is analogous).

The proof covers declarations whose parameter types and return types have no
static parameters, and calls to which declarations are applicable without
coercion.
It assumes that the declarations visible at the call satisfy the overloading
rules, so that no two of them have the same parameter type; that each of them has
a body and that the bodies are well typed; that the subtype relation is sound,
so that the dynamic type of an argument is a subtype of its static type, and
transitive; and that every value of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is a
value of one of its listed types (\secref{trait-decls}).
The compiled type checker does not yet enforce the last assumption across
components: a type declared in a later component below a trait with static
parameters that stands between a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its
listed types escapes its check (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger), and where
the assumption fails the uniqueness proved below is not guaranteed.
The proof does not extend to declarations with static parameters, whose
instantiation keeps obligations of its own (\secref{resolving-overloading},
\chapref{type-inference}), nor to coercion (\secref{proof-coercion-resolution}),
and it is not a proof of the soundness of the whole type system.

Consider a static function call $\f(\As)$ at some program point $Z$
and its corresponding dynamic function call $\f(\Xs)$.  Let $\Delta$
be the set of parameter types of function declarations of $\f$ that
call returns belongs to the intersection of those return types.
The static call may have more than one most specific declaration: covering
gives a declaration that holds the value of the argument, not one whose
parameter type is a supertype of the static type of the argument.
\revision{revival-proof}{The Working Draft of February 2011 proved that
$|\sigma| = 1$ and $|\delta| = 1$ whenever $|\Sigma| \neq 0$, and that
$D \Ovrsubtype S$ where $\sigma = \set{S}$ and $\delta = \set{D}$, from a Meet
Rule that asks for a declaration on the intersection itself.
With the case of the Meet Rule in which declarations together cover the
intersection, the proof is revised: the lemmas of existence are kept, the
uniqueness of the most specific declaration for the static call is given up,
the uniqueness for the dynamic call is proved by a covering declaration, and
two steps replace the last theorem, the refinement of every declaration
applicable to the static call and the result type of the call.
The scope and the assumptions stated above are new.}

Where the static type of a call's argument stands between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, several declarations applicable to
the static call may each have no other applicable declaration more specific
than them (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
Such a call is not a static error: it dispatches to a declaration no less
specific than each of them, and where they, and every declaration more specific
than them that the call may run, have no static parameters, its type is the
intersection of their return types (\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}).
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 knew no such call:
it read a \KWD{comprises} clause as saying which types are below a trait, where
\secref{trait-decls} now says which values belong to it, so that a trait with
static parameters may stand unlisted between a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause and its listed types.}
Concrete function declarations must satisfy the overloading rules.
Unless \VAR{T} has a \KWD{comprises} clause (or is a tuple type, at least
one of whose entries has a \KWD{comprises} clause), this implies that some
concrete declaration for \VAR{f} must have argument type \VAR{T}.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that the
union of the argument types of the concrete declarations must be equal to
\VAR{T}; under a \KWD{comprises} clause read at the level of values
(\secref{trait-decls}) the union of the listed types covers \VAR{T} without being

Where the Meet Rule for functions asks for a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in
the scope, it is also satisfied by declarations in the scope whose parameter
types are each a subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover
$\Ps \inter \Qs$ (\secref{internal-types}): every value of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
is a value of the parameter type of one of them, for every value a program can
make, not only for the values a program does make.
Each such declaration is more specific than both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$, and
at run time it is applicable to every argument whose value its parameter type
holds.
Every pair of the covering declarations must satisfy the overloading rules in
turn, as every pair of the set must.
This case does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and
$\Qs$ define coercions: covering does not choose between two coercions.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked for a
declaration on the intersection itself, and the draft note above asked what the
intersection of two declarations is.
The answer is the one the team's list of proposed features records for two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, ``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to
address this with the coverage check''.
It is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011, which asks
for a declaration on the meet; the paper of 2019 has no traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses.
Where a trait with static parameters stands between two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses and their listed types, the intersection of the two is
not equal to a named type (\secref{internal-types}), and only declarations that
together cover it can disambiguate them.
The coverage is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
subtype of another (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).}
